vignette:
A Matter of Respect

Samuel has been the principal of Riverside Secondary School for thirty-two years. His office walls hold photographs spanning three decades-graduation ceremonies, sports teams, scholarship recipients. He knows the names of nearly every student who passes through the school's gates, remembers their parents, asks about their futures. This job has defined him. When people in the community see him at the market or the mosque, they nod with recognition. "Principal Samuel," they say, with a certain deference he has earned through consistent presence and genuine care.

Eighteen months ago, everything fractured.

It was a Tuesday afternoon in March. Samuel was locking up the administration building when a former student-a young man expelled three years prior for bringing a weapon to school-appeared at his office door. Samuel remembers feeling no immediate alarm. He had handled countless difficult conversations over the decades. He invited the man inside, offered him a seat, asked what had brought him back.

The conversation lasted perhaps two minutes before the young man's fist connected with Samuel's face. What followed was a blur of violence that Samuel struggles to articulate even now. He was knocked to the ground, kicked repeatedly. His glasses shattered. He tasted blood. A security guard eventually intervened, but those moments-the helplessness, the shock of his body being used against his will-have remained lodged inside him like shrapnel.

Samuel recovered physically within weeks. The fractured ribs healed. The cuts faded. But something else did not mend.

Now, seventeen months later, Samuel finds himself hypervigilant in his own office. His door, once always open to students and staff, remains locked. He has rearranged his desk so his back is never to the entrance. He cannot sit comfortably during staff meetings; he positions himself near exits. When unexpected knocks come at his door, his heart races violently. His wife tells him he sometimes wakes at night, breathing heavily, his body drenched in sweat from dreams he cannot quite remember.

The school feels different now. Samuel notices faces in hallways and wonders about their intentions. He has become suspicious of students he once knew well. A raised voice in the corridor sends a jolt of adrenaline through his chest. He finds himself avoiding the cafeteria, the assembly hall, anywhere he might feel trapped or surrounded. His colleagues have noticed his withdrawal but attribute it to age, to the normal winding down before retirement.

What they do not see is the grinding exhaustion. Samuel lies awake at night, his mind cycling through the assault, imagining different outcomes. He replays the moments before-could he have seen it coming? Should he have been more cautious? The self-recrimination mingles with rage at the young man, at himself, at the unfairness of it all.

He has taken extended leave twice since the incident, telling the school board he needed rest. In truth, he cannot face returning. The thought of sitting in that office, of being vulnerable again in the space where the assault occurred, generates a dread so intense that his chest tightens and his breathing becomes shallow.

His wife worries. She sees him staring out the window for hours, sees how he flinches when she touches his shoulder unexpectedly. Samuel knows she is frightened by the distance growing between them, by his irritability, by the way he has withdrawn from the community life they once shared.

He wonders if he will ever feel safe again, or if this hypervigilance, this constant scanning for threat, has become his permanent state. He wonders who he is now, without the role that has sustained him.
